analysis.one_liner: Extends federal overtime pay and minimum-wage protections to farmworkers, who are currently excluded.
analysis.headline: Introduced in August 2026 with 13 Senate cosponsors, all Democrats or allied independents, and referred to the Senate labor committee; no further action and no vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would end a decades-old carve-out that leaves farmworkers out of the federal overtime rules that apply to most other workers. It would require overtime pay above a weekly threshold that starts at 55 hours and steps down to 40 hours over several years, with a later start for farms with 25 or fewer employees. It would also remove most of the Fair Labor Standards Act exemptions that currently spare agricultural employers from minimum-wage and recordkeeping rules, keeping only a small exemption for immediate family members. The bill was introduced by Senator Padilla with 13 cosponsors and referred to the Senate labor committee; no further action has been taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly two million farmworkers — many of whom work 60-plus-hour weeks during planting and harvest — would gain the right to overtime pay at 1.5 times their regular rate once weekly hours exceed a threshold that drops from 55 to 40 over several years. They would also gain minimum-wage and recordkeeping protections currently withheld through industry-specific exemptions, and the rules would cover more farms by tightening the small-farm exemption to operations using more than 500 man-days of labor. Farmworkers are among the lowest-paid workers in the country, so the change would meaningfully raise take-home pay for the heaviest workweeks.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Fair Labor Standards Act to require overtime pay (1.5 times the regular rate) for agricultural workers, phased in from 55 hours per week in 2027 down to 40 hours by 2030 for larger employers, and later for employers with 25 or fewer workers.

Repeals the FLSA section that carves agricultural workers out of overtime protections, and strips most exemptions from minimum-wage and recordkeeping rules for farm labor, keeping only a narrow exemption for employers' immediate family members.
Aligns the Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act's small-farm exemption with the narrowed FLSA exemption, extending those worker-protection rules to more farms.

analysis.who_pays: Farm owners and labor contractors would pay overtime premiums and face new wage-and-hour compliance and recordkeeping costs, with the burden phased in later for operations with 25 or fewer employees. Some of that cost would pass through to consumers as slightly higher food prices, and some growers might reduce hours or speed mechanization to avoid the premium.

drawbacks.text: Farm employers would face sharply higher labor costs, especially during harvests when long hours are common, and some warn of reduced hours, mechanization, or higher food prices; the bill acknowledges this by phasing the overtime threshold down to 40 hours over four years and delaying the start date for employers with 25 or fewer workers to 2030-2033.

Even after passage, farmworkers would wait years for full coverage: overtime at 55 hours only beginning January 1, 2027 at the earliest under the bill's schedule, with the complete set of exemptions removed only in 2030 for larger employers and 2033 for smaller ones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real and long overdue in policy terms: farmworkers are currently excluded from overtime rights most other workers have had since 1938, and phasing the requirement in over several years with a smaller-employer delay softens the shock. The acknowledged costs fall on farm businesses and, indirectly, on consumers through slightly higher food prices, and some growers argue seasonal harvest economics make overtime unworkable without cuts to base hours. The bill's very long phase-in also means a farmworker in 2028 still has no overtime right at 55 hours. The larger problem is the bill's prospects: it has no Republican support and sits in a committee controlled by the opposing party, so it is unlikely to advance.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate labor committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 6, 2026 and the same day was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, the standard first step for a Senate bill.
That referral is the last action on record; the committee has not scheduled a hearing or markup and the Senate has not taken the bill up.
Congress remains in session until January 3, 2027, so the bill is technically alive, but a bill with no committee action this late in a session rarely moves.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Farm owners and agricultural employers, who keep the current exemptions from overtime and related rules as long as the bill goes nowhere.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Growers keep the overtime exemption for now

for.name: Sen. Alex Padilla
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and authored its text extending overtime and minimum-wage protections to farmworkers.

for.name: 13 Senate cosponsors
for.role: 12 of 45 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Sanders, Warren, Booker, Markey, Blumenthal, and Wyden.

against.name: Agricultural industry groups
against.what_they_did: Long opposed extending federal overtime rules to agriculture, citing harvest-season labor costs; no organized Senate support for the bill exists.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the 55 Republican senators cosponsored the bill, and they control the committee where it was referred.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors are Democrats or allied independents and none of the 55 Republican senators support the bill, so the bill splits entirely on party lines.

industries.industry: Farm owners and agricultural employers (fruit, vegetable, and crop producers)
industries.note: The bill removes their exemption from federal overtime rules, requiring 1.5x pay above a phased-down weekly threshold, a direct cost increase that they would otherwise not bear. Large producers absorb it; small farms get a delay to 2030-2033.

industries.industry: Farm labor contractors and crew leaders
industries.note: The bill strips the exemptions under FLSA sections 13(b)(12)-(16) and (h)-(j) that currently relieve these intermediaries from minimum-wage and recordkeeping requirements, exposing them to wage-and-hour liability.
Higher farm labor costs would flow modestly into food prices over the phase-in period; in exchange, the workers who pick the food gain overtime rights the rest of the workforce already has.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to the Senate HELP Committee without bipartisan cosponsors almost never get a hearing or markup, especially in a session's final months; the most likely path is that the bill dies in committee when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027, unless it is attached to a larger package.
